articles.title: Live Meeting API Approach — Ordered Captions Through Durable Fan-Out
articles.excerpt: The page should fire when caption delivery is falling behind the meeting, not when the speech recognizer or WebSocket process happens to look busy. The least complex sound design is a two-stage pipeli…
articles.body: The page should fire when caption delivery is falling behind the meeting, not when the speech recognizer or WebSocket process happens to look busy. The least complex sound design is a two-stage pipeline: transcribe each meeting once, assign every finalized caption a monotonic sequence, then publish that event through a bounded fan-out layer with reconnect backfill. The same rule applies to a marketplace operations dashboard streaming device status: acquisition and subscriber delivery are separate failure domains, so measure them separately. A useful page might say caption_publish_lag SLO burn: 14 meetings affected, oldest unacknowledged sequence 1842 . The on-call can see user impact, scope, and a recovery cursor. A page saying websocket goroutines high offers none of those things.

articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Give the marketplace pipeline two small Express endpoints: liveness says the Node.js process can answer, while readiness says this instance can accept a run. Poll through the external route, re…
articles.body: TL;DR: Give the marketplace pipeline two small Express endpoints: liveness says the Node.js process can answer, while readiness says this instance can accept a run. Poll through the external route, retain every sanitized 5xx, and keep compact run summaries longer than verbose success events. The bill is ingestion, indexed fields, retained bytes, query work, and alert evaluation. Start with events per run × encoded bytes × retained runs × storage overhead . In a planning example, not a benchmark, 8 million offers emitting four 700-byte events produce 22.4 GB per run and 672 GB across 30 runs before indexing or replication. One terminal event per offer is 5.6 GB; 10,000 sampled successes at four events add 28 MB. Event elimination moves the dominant term.

articles.body: Here’s a question. Imagine you wake up tomorrow, and coding is completely solved. You tell an AI what you want to build, and it builds it. 99.9% accuracy. It maintains the code. It fixes its own bugs. It handles updates. It solves problems on its own. All you have to do is describe what you want. Would you still learn to code? Would you still spend hours debugging? Would you still study data structures and algorithms? Would you still care about what’s happening under the hood? Or would you simply move on to the next thing? Because if all you ever wanted was to write code, maybe AI could replace the part you enjoyed. But if you wanted to solve problems, build things that matter, understand how systems work, and turn ideas into reality… Maybe coding was never the destination.

articles.title: Binary One’s Complement: Definition, Formula, and Examples
articles.excerpt: Binary One’s Complement is an important concept in computer science and digital electronics. It is a method of obtaining the complement of a binary number by changing every 0 to 1 and every 1 to 0. Th…
articles.body: Binary One’s Complement is an important concept in computer science and digital electronics. It is a method of obtaining the complement of a binary number by changing every 0 to 1 and every 1 to 0. This simple operation is useful in binary arithmetic, digital logic, and the historical representation of signed integers in computers. Understanding one’s complement makes it easier to learn two’s complement, binary subtraction, and how computers represent positive and negative numbers. What Is Binary One’s Complement? One’s complement is the result of inverting every bit in a binary number. A binary number uses only two digits: 0 and 1. To calculate its one’s complement, replace each digit with its opposite. 0 becomes 1. 1 becomes 0. For example, the one’s complement of 101100 is 010011.

articles.title: Hand Off a FlutterFlow App to a Developer: What to Prepare
articles.excerpt: Your FlutterFlow app is on TestFlight, maybe live in the stores, and real people use it. You've found a developer to take it further, and their first message is: "Can you share the code and give me ac…
articles.body: Your FlutterFlow app is on TestFlight, maybe live in the stores, and real people use it. You've found a developer to take it further, and their first message is: "Can you share the code and give me access?" On mobile, that one request covers six or seven things: the FlutterFlow project, a GitHub repo, a Firebase or Supabase backend, Apple and Google developer accounts, push-notification keys and every third-party API the app calls. Hand off a FlutterFlow app to a developer without mapping those, and you'll either pay them to dig through your setup or give away something you can't get back. This guide covers what you can export, what to share instead of transfer, and what to write down first. TL;DR FlutterFlow gives you real code. Most mobile no-code tools don't.
